title.en: Type-Safe Agents: Validating LLM Output Like Pydantic AI

description.en: LLMs return text; your app needs trustworthy data. Pydantic AI's whole pitch is validated, typed output. Build the tiny validator at its core and never trust a raw model response again.

story_variants.en:
## The Problem With Trusting a Language Model

"An LLM will happily tell you a user's age is `"forty-two"`, or `42.0`, or forget the field entirely," Vaathiyaar warns. "Feed that straight into your database and it explodes at 3am. This is why **Pydantic AI** became one of 2026's most-loved agent frameworks: it refuses to hand you output until it has been **validated against a schema** and coerced into real Python types."

### Schemas Are Contracts

A schema says: *this field is required, and it must be this type.* Pydantic AI turns the model's loose JSON into a checked object — or raises a clear error listing exactly what's wrong — so the rest of your code can trust its inputs.

```
schema = {"name": str, "age": int}
raw    = {"name": "Ada", "age": "42"}   # age is a STRING from the LLM
```

A good validator does three things:
1. **Checks presence** — every required field is there.
2. **Coerces** — `"42"` becomes `42` when the target is `int` (LLMs love quoting numbers).
3. **Rejects the impossible** — `"forty-two"` can't become an int, so it fails loudly.

### Why Coercion Matters

The single most common LLM output bug is the *stringified number*. The model returns `"age": "42"` because JSON came out of a text generator. A validator that coerces `"42" -> 42` silently fixes the 90% case, while still rejecting genuine garbage like `"forty-two"`.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** never let a raw model response cross into your business logic. Validate at the boundary — exactly once — and everything downstream gets to assume clean, typed data.

Today you build that boundary: a `validate(data, schema)` that returns a clean, coerced dict or raises on anything it can't honestly fix.

explanation.en: Walk the contract: each field name and its required type

steps.line: if field not in data: raise ValueError(...)

explanation.en: A missing required field fails immediately and clearly
Coerce: int('42') -> 42. If it can't, Python raises for us

instruction.en: Implement `validate(data, schema)` — the boundary that makes agent output trustworthy. `schema` maps field names to types, e.g. `{"name": str, "age": int}`. For each field: raise `ValueError` if it is missing, otherwise **coerce** the value with its type (so `"42"` becomes `42`). Return a new dict of the coerced values. Then print `validate({"name": "Ada", "age": "42"}, {"name": str, "age": int})`.

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def validate(data: dict, schema: dict) -> dict:
    """Return a dict with every schema field present and coerced to its type.
    Raise ValueError if a required field is missing."""
    # for field, typ in schema.items():
    #   - missing? raise ValueError(f"missing '{field}'")
    #   - else coerce: typ(data[field])
    pass

print(validate({"name": "Ada", "age": "42"}, {"name": str, "age": int}))

en: Loop: for field, typ in schema.items()
Coerce by calling the type: typ(data[field]) turns '42' into 42
TypeError: can't add str and int
ta: TypeError: str மற்றும் int-ஐ கூட்ட முடியாது

q.en: With schema {"age": int}, the LLM returns "age": "forty-two". What should a good validator do?
q.ta: schema {"age": int} எனும்போது, LLM "age": "forty-two" எனத் தருகிறது. ஒரு நல்ல validator என்ன செய்ய வேண்டும்?

q.en: Spot the mistake: the validator loops with `for field, typ in schema:` over a dict schema. What's wrong?
q.ta: தவறைக் கண்டுபிடி: validator ஒரு dict schema மீது `for field, typ in schema:` என loop செய்கிறது. என்ன தவறு?

en: Looping a dict gives only keys; use schema.items()
Dicts can't be looped over at all
It should be `for typ, field in schema:`
ta: dict-ஐ loop செய்தால் keys மட்டுமே வரும்; schema.items() பயன்படுத்து
`for typ, field in schema:` என்று இருக்க வேண்டும்
தவறு இல்லை; அது (field, type) ஜோடிகளைத் தரும்

q.en: Following the lesson, what happens with validate({"name": "Ada"}, {"name": str, "age": int})?
q.ta: பாடத்தின்படி, validate({"name": "Ada"}, {"name": str, "age": int}) இயக்கினால் என்ன நடக்கும்?

under_the_hood.summary: A type-safe agent checks the model's output against a schema before using it: every required field must be present, values are coerced to the declared type where safe ('42' -> 42) and rejected where not ('forty-two'), and only a validated object is passed on.

steps.title: A schema is a contract
steps.body: schema = {'name': str, 'age': int} states which fields must exist and what type each must have. Downstream code is written against this contract, not against whatever the model happened to produce.

steps.title: Check presence
steps.body: Walk the schema; for each field missing from the model's data raise ValueError('missing age'). A missing field is caught here instead of as a KeyError deep in the application.

steps.title: Coerce where it is safe
steps.body: int('42') succeeds, so '42' becomes 42. int('forty-two') raises, so the value is rejected rather than guessed. Pydantic's default (lax) mode follows the same idea: it converts unambiguous representations and refuses the rest.

steps.title: Turn failures into retries
steps.body: Frameworks such as Pydantic AI send the validation error back to the model ('age: input should be a valid integer') and ask again, up to a retry limit. Most format mistakes are fixed on the second try.

steps.title: Typed all the way down
steps.body: After validation the value is a real int and the object matches the schema, so type checkers and the rest of the code can rely on it. The untrusted text never reaches the database directly.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Treat model output like user input: validate against a schema, coerce only what is unambiguous, and retry or fail loudly on the rest.
